newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan seen facing pointed questions in House.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan seen facing pointed questions in House.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, having warned about imbalances that may threaten the U.S. expansion, is likely to face pointed questions about an eventual interest rate hike when he returns to Capitol Hill on Wednesday.

"The question-and-answer session was not pointed because the Senate was very easy on him, in part because Greenspan is held in such high regard in Congress," said William Dudley, chief economist at Goldman, Sachs and Co. while referring to Greenspan's first part of the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.
"Members of the House Banking Committee members are surely going to be more informed because they had a week for their staff to have the testimony," Dudley added.

The Fed chairman sounded words of caution before the Senate about potential imbalances that may endanger the long-toothed expansion. He is expected to deliver the same testimony on Wednesday before the House Banking Committee.
Analysts said the benefit of such insight about Greenspan's concern should lead House Banking Committee members to press Greenspan more aggressively on the monetary policy outlook.
"Greenspan is obviously worried that markets have built in too good a view about the sustainability of the expansion," Goldman's Dudley noted.
Greenspan warned of "asset-price inflation that can feed through into markets for goods and services."
Nomura Securities International chief economist David Resler said Greenspan clearly pointed a finger at financial markets' overvaluation as a potential source of imbalance.
"There is no question that Greenspan in his testimony last week did not present a profile of the economy that would seem to require any adjustment of policy," Resler said.

"A small tightening would be a bit of insurance against the possibility of imbalances resulting from market exhuberance," Resler added. "What will be interesting is the question 'Where do you get off being the final arbitrator.'"
Resler expected Greenspan to state the Fed does not concern itself with asset price levels but does take into account the impact financial markets have on the economy.

Resler said rapid gains on paper may fuel consumer confidence and spending beyond a sustainable pace while abrupt market corrections may set a negative psychology resulting in a sudden economic slowdown.
Ken Bercuson, head of research at SBC Warburg, saw imbalances developing in both financial and labor markets and expected Greenspan to reiterate his views on the issues.

"Financial markets obviously are one area where Greenspan thinks there is an imbalance due to the wealth effect. They are like a ticking bomb. They yet have to engender too rapid a pace of spending, but eventually they will," Bercuson said. "The most severe imbalances are in the labor markets."
Bercuson expected Greenspan to underline "the cost of waiting, because if you wait too long, the imbalances would become a lot more severe."
Stephen Axilrod, a former Fed Board staff director, expected Greenspan to focus on the stock market as a potential source of imbalance to the U.S. economy.
"The only imbalance is the stock market, and the imbalance is only in reference to earning expectations," Axilrod, now an adviser with MFR Inc., said.
"If the market goes too far ahead, you could have a sharp drop which, in turn, could affect the economy in a pretty sharp manner," he added.
